extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students studying mathematical logic and formal proof systems
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and formal results for building and reasoning about deductions in first-order logic: axioms (tautologies, quantifier axioms, equality), rules (modus ponens, generalization, deduction), substitution/substitutability, and metatheorems (soundness, strategies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitutability of a term for a variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Let x be a variable, t a term. We define the phrase 't is substitutable for x in α' as follows: 1. For atomic α, t is always substitutable for x in α. 2. t is substitutable for x in (¬ α) iff it is substitutable for x in α. t is substitutable for x in (α → β) iff it is substitutable for x in both α and β. 3. t is substitutable for x in ∀ y α iff either (a) x does not occur free in ∀ y α, or (b) y does not occur in t and t is substitutable for x in α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recursive definition prevents quantifier capture. Examples: x is always substitutable for itself. If t contains no variables occurring in α then t is substitutable. Even if t is not substitutable, one may still form α_x^t syntactically, but that may be unwise (danger: captured variables and false sentences). The definition is designed for use in inductive proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom group 2 (quantifier-instantiation axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Axiom group 2 consists of all generalizations of formulas of the form ∀ x α → α_x^t, where the term t is substitutable for the variable x in the formula α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and non-examples are given: a formula like ∀ v3( ∀ v1(Av1 → ∀ v2 Av2) → (Av2 → ∀ v2 Av2)) is in axiom group 2 (here x=v1, t=v2). But ∀ v1 ∀ v2 Bv1v2 → ∀ v2 Bv2v2 is not in axiom group 2 since v2 is not substitutable for v1 in ∀ v2 Bv1v2. The substitutability restriction is essential to avoid quantifier capture (see Example 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom group 1 (tautologies of sentential logic lifted to FOL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Axiom group 1 consists of generalizations of the tautologies of sentential logic (using only ¬ and →) obtained by replacing each sentence symbol by a wff of the first-order language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate viewpoint: take prime formulas (atomic and ∀ x α) as sentential atoms; any sentential tautology using these atoms is in axiom group 1. Example: ( ∀ y ¬ P y → ¬ P x) → (P x → ¬ ∀ y ¬ P y) is such a generalization. The set of tautologies is a decidable set (useful for enumerability), but including all tautologies as axioms is overkill; one could use a smaller decidable subset and derive others by modus ponens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of tautologies / decidability tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking all tautologies as logical axioms is overkill; we could reduce axiom group 1 to a subset of tautologies for which we have fast (polynomial-time) decision procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing the axiom set shortens the axiom list but lengthens derivations. The text notes the tautologies form a nice decidable set (important for enumerability), but there is no known fast decision procedure for tautologies in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ ⊢ φ and x does not occur free in any formula in Γ, then Γ ⊢ ∀ x φ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction: show the set {ϕ | Γ ⊢ ∀ x ϕ} contains Γ ∪ (logical axioms) and is closed under modus ponens. The restriction that x not occur free in Γ is essential (counterexamples exist otherwise). The theorem also supplies an effective method to transform a deduction of φ from Γ into a deduction of ∀ x φ from Γ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule T (Lemma 24C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ ⊢ α1, ..., Γ ⊢ αn and {α1,...,αn} tautologically implies β, then Γ ⊢ β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: α1 → ··· → αn → β is a tautology (hence a logical axiom); apply modus ponens n times. This rule is used frequently to combine earlier derived formulas into a new consequence when a sentential tautology yields the implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ; γ ⊢ ϕ, then Γ ⊢ (γ → ϕ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The converse also holds (by modus ponens). Two proofs are given: one uses sentential compactness (semantic/tautological argument), the other is syntactic and shows how to transform a deduction of ϕ from Γ∪{γ} into a deduction of γ → ϕ from Γ via induction on the derivation of ϕ. This theorem is a principal tool for moving assumptions into antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraposition corollary (24D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Γ; ϕ ⊢ ¬ ψ iff Γ; ψ ⊢ ¬ ϕ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived using the deduction theorem and Rule T together with the sentential tautology that ϕ → ¬ ψ tautologically implies ψ → ¬ ϕ. The equivalence holds by symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reductio ad absurdum (24E)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ; ϕ is inconsistent (i.e., for some β both β and ¬ β are theorems of Γ; ϕ), then Γ ⊢ ¬ ϕ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: from inconsistency obtain Γ ⊢ ϕ → β and Γ ⊢ ϕ → ¬β; these tautologically imply Γ ⊢ ¬ ϕ by sentential reasoning. This is the formal counterpart of proof by contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax-driven proof-construction strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: When attempting to show Γ ⊢ ϕ, useful starting points depend on the syntactic form of ϕ: 1) If ϕ is (ψ → θ), it suffices to show Γ; ψ ⊢ θ. 2) If ϕ is ∀ x ψ and x not free in Γ, it suffices to show Γ ⊢ ψ (variations handled by re-replacement lemma). 3) If ϕ is a negation, there are subcases: a) ¬(ψ → θ): show Γ ⊢ ψ and Γ ⊢ ¬θ; b) ¬¬ψ: show Γ ⊢ ψ; c) ¬ ∀ x ψ: try to show Γ ⊢ ¬ ψ_x^t for some t substitutable for x, but this may fail — use contraposition or reductio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes working backward and using the deduction and generalization theorems, contraposition, and reductio ad absurdum as tactics. It warns that for ¬ ∀ x ψ one cannot always find a substitutable term t to instantiate, and provides alternates (contraposition, RAA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule EI (existential instantiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume c is a constant symbol that does not occur in ϕ, ψ, or Γ, and Γ; ϕ_x^c ⊢ ψ. Then Γ; ∃ x ϕ ⊢ ψ, and there is a deduction of ψ from Γ; ∃ x ϕ in which c does not occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'EI' formalizes reasoning from 'there exists x such that ϕ' by introducing a fresh constant c and reasoning from ϕ[c/x]. Caveat: EI does not assert ∃ x ϕ ⊢ ϕ_x^c (this is usually false). The rule is primarily a technical convenience (existential instantiation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetic variants and avoidance of substitutability failure (Theorem 24I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a formula ϕ, term t, and variable x, one can find a formula ϕ' (differing from ϕ only by choice of bound variable names) such that (a) ϕ ⊢ ϕ' and ϕ' ⊢ ϕ, and (b) t is substitutable for x in ϕ'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction proceeds by recursion on ϕ: when bound variable y conflicts with variables of t, rename to a fresh z and propagate. This allows avoiding quantifier capture by producing logically equivalent 'alphabetic variants'. Typical strategy: replace quantifiers to make substitution legal; proofs show logical equivalence and substitutability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality axiom Eq1 (reflexivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eq1: ⊢ ∀ x x = x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from axiom group 5. Equality is reflexive in all structures; this axiom is used throughout proofs about equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality axiom Eq2 (symmetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eq2: ⊢ ∀ x ∀ y(x = y → y = x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved earlier (page 122). Equality's symmetry is derivable from axiom group 6 and other axioms; used to show equality is an equivalence relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality axiom Eq3 (transitivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eq3: ⊢ ∀ x ∀ y ∀ z(x = y → y = z → x = z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise-proved (Exercise 11). Together with Eq1 and Eq2 this establishes equality as an equivalence relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality compatibility with predicates (Eq4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an n-place predicate symbol P: ⊢ ∀ x1 ... ∀ xn ∀ y1 ... ∀ yn (x1 = y1 → ... → xn = yn → (P x1...xn → P y1...yn)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by showing from hypotheses x1 = y1, ..., P x1...xn one can deduce P y1...yn using members of axiom group 6. This establishes that equal arguments may be substituted in predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality compatibility with functions (Eq5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an n-place function symbol f: ⊢ ∀ x1 ... ∀ xn ∀ y1 ... ∀ yn (x1 = y1 → ... → xn = yn → f x1...xn = f y1...yn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved similarly to Eq4 (see example on page 122). Ensures functions respect equality by producing equal function-values from equal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution lemma and Lemma 25B (commutation of substitution and assignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 25B: For any term u, s(u_x^t) = s(x | s(t))(u). Substitution Lemma: If term t is substitutable for variable x in ϕ, then |=_A ϕ_x^t [s] iff |=_A ϕ[s(x | s(t))].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These lemmas formalize that substituting a term into a formula corresponds to evaluating the formula under an assignment modified so x maps to the value of the term. They are essential for the semantic proof of axiom group 2 validity and for the Soundness Theorem. Proofs proceed by induction on term u and formula ϕ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ ⊢ ϕ, then Γ |= ϕ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline: show every logical axiom is valid (Lemma 25A), and that modus ponens preserves validity. Then use induction on derivations: axioms valid, members of Γ trivially valid, and modus ponens preserves logical implication. Substitution lemma is used to handle quantifier-instantiation axioms (axiom group 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductions built from logical axioms, nonlogical axioms, and modus ponens
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems of a set Γ are those built up from Γ ∪ (logical axioms) by repeated application of modus ponens; explicit derivations can be represented as pedigree trees compressible into linear sequences (deductions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show constructing deductions (e.g., P x → ∃ y P y) by assembling axioms and applying modus ponens. The text emphasizes that the meta-language 'proof' often sketches a deduction and that actual shortest formal deductions may be longer (e.g., a claimed 17-formula shortest deduction for a sample theorem).
